newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan output data dampens rate hike expectations.
newsitem.headline: Japan output data dampens rate hike expectations.

text.p: Japan's industrial production figure for April showed an unexpected decline Thursday, dampening market expectations of an early interest rate increase based on a brighter economic outlook.

"For the markets, the message should be very simple and straightforward: This number underscores that the Bank of Japan is not going to be in a hurry to hike interest rates in the next three to six months," Jesper Koll, head of research at J.P. Morgan, Tokyo, told Reuters Financial Television.
Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry said April industrial output fell a preliminary 0.4 percent from the previous month on a seasonally adjusted basis.

An MITI official told reporters that output in the April-to-June period was expected to fall 0.7 percent from the previous quarter, although compared with the same period a year ago, it would register a gain of 6.1 percent.
The official attributed the dip in production in April to a rise in Japan's sales tax to 5 percent from 3 percent on April 1 and to a slip in production from orders.

Financial markets responded quickly to the weaker-than-expected data, with Euroyen futures, the dollar and Japanese government bonds all leaping on the news as expectations of an early Japanese rate rise faded.
Currency traders said the dollar rose to about 116.48 yen in afternoon trade as the yield of Japanese government bonds kept slipping after the data.

The market had been speculating that an early rise in the Japan's official discount rate was possible after the Bank of Japan said late Wednesday that it would release its next "tankan" survey of corporate sentiment on June 25, rather than in early July.
The central bank has kept the discount rate -- at which it lends to commercial banks -- at a record-low 0.5 percent since September 1995, in an effort to stimulate economic recovery.
Despite the markets' reaction to Thursday's data, some economists doubted whether expectations of a rate hike had competely disappeared.

"There's no change in the fact that the BOJ will change its monetary policy somewhere along the line and it's hard to imagine that expectations of a rate hike will recede drastically just with the industrial output data," said Yukinobu Kaibe, manager of the treasury planning division at Nippon Credit Bank.
